title: Guardians of the Unwritten Constitution: Lord Case's Evidence
label: 16 September 2026 · Lord Case on constitutional safeguards
summary: Lord Case, former Cabinet Secretary, told the Constitution Committee that the Cabinet Secretary is a 'tier 2' constitutional guardian who advises the Prime Minister but lacks independent legal power. He described how the 'golden triangle' works in normal times and how it responded during the final days of Boris Johnson's premiership. He argued that the constitution is vulnerable to governments ignoring precedent, called the 'good chaps' theory inadequate, and said he now favours moving towards a more codified, written constitution, though he acknowledged this would be very difficult to achieve outside a major national crisis.

speakers.label: Lord Case
speakers.name: Lord Case
speakers.role: Former Cabinet Secretary and Head of the Civil Service, UK Government

speakers.label: Committee Member
speakers.name: Committee Member
speakers.role: Combines repetitive questions from Lord Beith, Lord Burnett of Maldon, Lord Cryer, Lord Bellamy, Lord Jones of Penybont, Baroness Hamwee, Lord Murphy of Torfaen and Baroness Laing of Elderslie

chapters.title: The Cabinet Secretary as Tier 2 Guardian
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case says the Cabinet Secretary is a constitutional guardian, but a lesser one than the monarch or Prime Minister, with no legal power of their own.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord Case, welcome. Let's start generally: what's the role of the Cabinet Secretary in how the UK constitution works? Would you call the Cabinet Secretary a constitutional guardian?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Good morning, Chair. Yes, the Cabinet Secretary is one of the constitutional guardians, but I'd describe the role as a tier 2 guardian, not tier 1.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The tier 1 guardians are really the monarch and the Prime Minister. People like the Cabinet Secretary, the PM's principal private secretary and the sovereign's private secretary don't have much legal status separate from their bosses. They're the support cast to those principal figures.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Your main job is to advise the Prime Minister on constitutional matters. Occasionally you get drawn into conversations with the sovereign, or more likely the sovereign's private secretary, but that's rarer.

chapters.title: Navigating Four Prime Ministers and Hard Moments
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case says trust, access to predecessors and a strong personal grounding are essential when the constitutional chips are down, citing how he used the 'Senex' letter to block an ill-advised snap election.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You served under four Prime Ministers in quick succession. How did you navigate complex or novel constitutional issues during that time?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I suspect most of the lessons are about the internal operation of political parties rather than the constitution itself. During my time we had a change of monarch, four Prime Ministers, a global pandemic that put enormous strain on the devolution settlement—plenty going on constitutionally.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: At the heart of navigating these things is a trusting relationship with your key colleagues and access to your predecessors. I was lucky enough to study under people like Lord Hennessy, so I had some academic training in thinking about the constitution.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Let me give you an example. On those couple of extraordinary days when Boris Johnson's Cabinet ministers were resigning left, right and centre, some uninformed individual around him floated the idea of calling a general election to avoid him being brought down by his own party.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: That was a classic moment where you have to get out the Lascelles principles and the 'Senex' letter, show them and say: 'Here are all the reasons why I don't think that's a very good idea and why the sovereign might be within their rights to refuse to allow you to call a general election, so don't pursue that line.'

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Does that mean the Cabinet Secretary has to have access to predecessors and be strong enough to stand up to a powerful Cabinet Minister who thinks public opinion is on his side?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes, you do. You need to be very confident of your ground, know what are facts, what's your judgment and what's opinion, and be willing to explain that to a Prime Minister, a Cabinet Minister or whoever.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So it sounds like there's an informal body of experienced people providing a sort of guardianship of the constitution.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I would say so. But I'll declare a broader view now: I think it's inadequate. I started as a PhD student under Lord Hennessy celebrating the glories of our unwritten constitution, but I've become more and more convinced we should be heading towards a more codified and written constitution.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Having seen the constitution up close and personal, I absolutely loathe the 'good chaps' phrase. Nearly all the people who operated in these guardian roles were chaps, and 'chaps' was a good description because many of them had been to school together, university together, came from the same social classes and backgrounds. I don't think that's a justifiable way of managing a 21st-century G7 economy.

chapters.title: Weaknesses, Resignation and the Unelected
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case says the Cabinet Secretary's main weakness is being hired and fired by the Prime Minister, and that unelected officials, including the monarch, must ultimately give way to an elected government with a manifesto mandate.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Does the Cabinet Secretary have weaknesses as a constitutional guardian? If you couldn't persuade a Prime Minister that something was fundamentally wrong, at what point would you resign?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes, there are inherent weaknesses. It comes down to the fact that you're appointed and dismissed at the will of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is the boss; the Cabinet Secretary is an adviser. If the Prime Minister ignores your advice, in extremis they could dismiss you and bring in someone who'll give different advice.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Or the Cabinet Secretary could say: 'You're not listening. This isn't just a policy difference, this is a critical point of constitutional safety, so I'm going to resign over this.' You could imagine that. But in the modern cut and thrust of British politics, I'm not entirely sure a Cabinet Secretary's resignation would have that impact any more. We come and go a bit like London buses.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: But there's a difference between being sacked and walking out saying, 'I'm going because you're making a major constitutional mistake.' Wouldn't that have an impact?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It would, and it depends on personalities and context. But that's one of the reasons I've become more convinced we need to head much further down the road of codifying these things. Leaving it to the chance of a Cabinet Secretary resigning and making the right fuss on the way out feels like a rather unreliable way of alerting the nation that something seriously constitutionally unwise is going on.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: And if something is in a recently elected government's manifesto but is constitutionally offensive, that would be much harder to block, wouldn't it?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I completely agree. If the Prime Minister of the day, supported by Cabinet and Parliament, is carrying out something on the basis of a manifesto, anybody unelected—whether sovereign or official—pretty much has to get out of the way.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Does that mean the monarchy itself is quite a weak constitutional safeguard in extreme circumstances?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In my view, yes.

chapters.title: Codification, the Cabinet Manual and the Deputy PM Gap
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case argues the Cabinet Manual is out of date and toothless, and that things like having a Deputy Prime Minister should be put into law instead of left to a Prime Minister's whim.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You've said you want a more codified constitution. Could you give examples of what could be put into legislation, or are you thinking of a full written constitution?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Personally, I'm at the more radical end. But I'm also a pragmatist—it'll be a very long time before we have a written constitution. You need a very particular set of circumstances for a nation to arrive at one. Around the world, written constitutions have only been born out of extreme circumstances. We're not there yet.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: A pragmatic approach is needed. Look at the Cabinet Manual—it's woefully out of date, ludicrously so. As Cabinet Secretary I produced an updated draft, now three or four Prime Ministers ago. All of them said they'd publish it, but it hasn't been done. It's crazy.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Even so, the Cabinet Manual has no authority or effect. It just sits there as a public document. That's not particularly wise. There are aspects of it worth bringing into legislation.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: One important example is the requirement to have a Deputy Prime Minister. After the episode where Boris Johnson could have ended up on a ventilator, we put arrangements in place to always have a Deputy PM. The Covid inquiry took evidence and agreed. But the current Prime Minister hasn't appointed one. It's still totally open to any Prime Minister to say 'no thanks'. For the safety and certainty of managing the nation, we shouldn't leave that to the whim of a Prime Minister of the day.

chapters.title: The Golden Triangle Under Strain
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case says the golden triangle is really a network of advisers to the Prime Minister and the sovereign, and that in a crisis they step up information-sharing and try to keep advice consistent.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What role does the principal private secretary to the Prime Minister play in constitutional decision-making?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: This is probably the least understood corner of the golden triangle. In my experience, the PM's principal private secretary is the much more frequent conduit between the Government and the sovereign—or the sovereign's staff. As PPS I'd be talking to my counterpart several times a week, all on the principle of 'no surprises'.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: That doesn't mean we were discussing grand constitutional crises multiple times a week. It's just the important flow of information: what's on the Prime Minister's mind, what's happening in a military campaign, what's going on in Parliament. Cabinet Secretary interactions are much fewer and usually only when you're crossing the threshold of a serious constitutional issue.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: How would the golden triangle operate if the engine is breaking down, not just lubricating a well-running machine?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Let me give a concrete example: those couple of days at the end of Boris Johnson's time when people were thinking about calling a general election to save his premiership. As soon as that came to me, I was immediately on the phone to other members of the golden triangle saying: 'There's something happening here we need to know about. We need to step up our golden triangle DEFCON level. Time to stand on alert.'

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The primary task of that group is exchanging information and triangulating advice: 'This is what I'm saying to the Prime Minister,' 'This is what I'm saying to the sovereign.' Can we make sure the facts on which we're drawing our advice are consistent, we're all aware of the same precedents and reading them the same way?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In the end, the golden triangle are advisers to two critical constitutional principals. We've given it this slightly silly name—the golden triangle—and elevated it in some constitutional fantasy league way, but the reality is all its members are advisers, not principals themselves.

chapters.title: Strengthening the Backstop Without Strengthening the Monarchy
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case says he wouldn't strengthen the monarch's role, and that the real answer is more inked lines—ideally a written constitution—rather than relying on Whitehall discretion.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said the monarch as a constitutional safeguard is on the weaker side. Would you choose to strengthen it, or is the real backstop in Whitehall or Parliament?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I wouldn't strengthen the role of the monarch. In a 21st-century modern democracy, strengthening the role of a beloved but still unelected Head of State would feel like going against the flow of our nation's history.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In terms of strengthening the backstop, it's the strength of that backstop that's led me on this strange journey to conclude that probably the best backstop is a written constitution.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I certainly don't think the backstop should be in the hands of anybody in Whitehall. It's important to have gatekeepers and guardians like Cabinet Secretaries, but these things ultimately need to rest in settled law.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Isn't there a contradiction? You argue for a written constitution where the monarch's role would be much more defined, but the strength of the present situation is that it isn't defined in writing.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: This is a wonderful essay question hammered out in seminar rooms all around the country. I learned my constitutional thinking under Peter Hennessy, and we celebrated the glories of our unwritten constitution and how that flexibility created strength.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: But I've seen it up close, and my experience fits with points that have come up in your previous sessions—about transparency, about who in this country wields power, in whose interests, who put them there and how you get rid of them if they aren't acting in the interests of the majority. Those factors have led me on this strange journey towards thinking a written constitution might, in the end, be the right answer.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Short of a written constitution, is there anything that could be done to strengthen our constitutional safeguards?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Identifying some of those critical things we might move from the precedent book or the Cabinet Manual and bringing them into legislation feels like a good idea.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Take the grand sweep of history: there's an enormously significant constitutional thing happening in Parliament right now—changing the law so a Roman Catholic or Jewish Prime Minister could be involved in appointing Church of England bishops. That's a really significant historical, constitutional and societal move.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: More seriously, I'd look at questions around the order of precedence: who do you call if X or Y is unavailable? We should take away the ambiguity and the assumptions. You wouldn't run a business like that, so why are we trying to run a country with this level of uncertainty?

chapters.title: Is the Constitution Vulnerable?
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case says the constitution is vulnerable because governments can ignore precedent and advice, and that while a written constitution would be hard to achieve, we need more inked lines rather than relying on personality and context.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Is the constitution overall vulnerable, and if so, in what ways?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Over recent years we've seen an amazing amount of freedom for a Government of the day to ignore precedent and ignore the advice drawn from that 'good faith' theory of the constitution.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Is it truly a growing trend? I don't know, but it feels like one to me. Things that used to be pencil lines in and around our constitution perhaps should be turned into inked lines. Even in a written constitution, personality and context will always be absolutely critical. I'm not remotely naive about politics.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I dug out this morning a quote from Leo Amery just after the war, describing the constitution as 'a living structure, continuously shaped in the course of history by the interaction of individual purposes and collective instincts with the requirements of ever-varying circumstances.' It's wonderful. But should we really be operating a 21st-century G7, P5, nuclear-armed state in that way? It would be good to have a few more inked lines.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: If we were to aim for a written constitution, how would we get from here to there? Would it gum up everything else that needs to happen?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It would be extremely difficult to achieve as part of the normal run of politics. The circumstances in which you shift to a written constitution come out of very large-scale national or international crisis—liberation moments where restating or creating a new platform for your national institutions really matters.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I'm highly pragmatic about how you'd get there. We see with the endless constitutional tinkering—take House of Lords reform—that the moment you go into that, it can gum everything up. I'd be very cautious about jumping all the way to a written constitution through the normal times of Parliament.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you very much, Lord Case. We've come to the end of our questions. I want to thank you for your time and for being very candid. I'm sure Lord Hennessy will be very pleased—and I'm sure he's listening in.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: He'll wildly disagree with large chunks of it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We're all unelected here as well, but we feel we have a role in shedding light on this. We're trying to look ahead 10 to 15 years at constitutional weaknesses and whether we need to strengthen safeguards. Is there anything else you'd like to finish on?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: No. Thank you very much. More power to your elbow.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thanks a lot. I now draw this session to a close.
